{{Short description|Swedish mathematician (1877–1932)}}
'''Thomas Hakon Grönwall''' or '''Thomas Hakon Gronwall''' (born '''Hakon Tomi Grönwall''';<ref name="Einar Hill" /> January 16, 1877 in Dylta bruk, [[Sweden]] – May 9, 1932 in [[New York City]], [[New York (state)|New York]]) was a [[:Category:Swedish mathematicians|Swedish mathematician]]. He studied at the [[University College of Stockholm]] and [[Uppsala University]] and completed his [[Ph.D.]] at Uppsala in 1898.  Grönwall worked for about a year as a civil engineer in Germany before he emigrated to the United States in 1904.  He later taught mathematics at [[Princeton University]] and from 1925 he was a member of the physics department at [[Columbia University]].<ref name="Einar Hill">{{cite journal|author=Hille, Einar|authorlink=Einar Hille|title=Thomas Hakon Gronwall—In memoriam|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1932|volume=38|issue=11|pages=775–786|mr=1562506|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1932-05492-1|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="MacTutor" />

In 1925 he started to collaborate with [[Victor LaMer]], which led to his joining the Department of Physics at Columbia University as an associate in 1927{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}}. {{According to whom|This connection was a great opportunity|date=July 2024}}. There were no teaching obligations; he had complete control of his own time and an abundance of new intriguing problems to address in physical chemistry and in atomic physics{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}}. He developed an analytical solution to the [[Poisson-Boltzmann equation]] as it appears in the [[Debye–Hückel theory]]<ref name="Einar Hill" />
